input: Generative models collapse the cost of producing content, and the scarce asset stops being supply and becomes distribution. When anyone can make an unlimited quantity of adequate material, the constraint moves to who can put it in front of people. Platforms that already own an audience capture the surplus, because they can fill more inventory at lower production cost without acquiring a single additional user. The value accrues to the pipe, not to what flows through it.

thesis.title: Distribution Scarcity: AI Shifts Value to the Pipe
thesis.summary: Generative AI commoditizes content production, making distribution the scarce resource. Platforms owning large, captive audiences can fill more ad inventory at near-zero marginal content cost, expanding margins without user acquisition spend. Meta, Alphabet, and Amazon are the clearest expressions: each owns a distribution moat that becomes more valuable as content supply becomes infinite. Microsoft's LinkedIn and Azure-backed Copilot ecosystem adds enterprise distribution leverage. The thesis is not about AI model quality — it is about who captures the surplus when content cost collapses.

holdings.rationale: Meta owns the largest social distribution pipe in the world. AI-generated content fills Reels and Feed inventory at near-zero cost, enabling higher ad load without proportional user growth. Its closed ecosystem means advertisers have no substitute for its audience density, giving Meta direct pricing power over the surplus generated by content commoditization.

Alphabet's Search and YouTube are the internet's primary discovery pipes. As generative content floods the web, Google's index and ranking authority becomes the gatekeeper for what surfaces. YouTube benefits from AI-assisted creation volume filling more inventory; Search monetizes the moment users need a signal amid the noise — a structural advantage that compounds as content supply grows.

S&P 500 anchors the basket in the deepest liquidity pool and captures broad market participation in the AI-driven productivity shift. The index's heavy weighting toward the same distribution platforms named in the thesis reinforces the primary view while keeping mint slippage manageable.

Nasdaq 100 concentrates exposure in tech and communication services — the sectors where distribution moats are most durable. Provides deep liquidity and captures the same platform-economy thesis through index-level exposure, reinforcing METAx and GOOGLx without adding thin-pool slippage.

Amazon's distribution thesis runs through Prime Video, Twitch, and its sponsored-products ad network. AI lowers the cost of filling Prime Video's slate and generating ad creative, expanding margin on inventory Amazon already owns. Its ad business is growing faster than its retail segment, and distribution ownership over 200M+ Prime households is the structural mechanism.

falsifier.claim: Platforms that own distribution capture the surplus when content production costs collapse — their ad revenue per user and operating margins expand as AI fills inventory.
falsifier.observable: Meta and Alphabet combined reported operating margin and revenue-per-user metrics in quarterly earnings, and their stated ad pricing (CPM/CPC trends) reported in each earnings call.
falsifier.breachCondition: Both Meta and Alphabet report flat or declining operating margins year-over-year for two consecutive quarters, or both report declining average revenue per user, indicating advertisers are not paying a premium for owned-pipe distribution.
